title: Outcome versus process focused future thinking: results from a randomised experiment.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Future thinking plays a central role in emotion and behaviour, yet different modes of simulation may have distinct effects. This pre-registered experiment compared outcome- and process-focused future thinking on affective and cognitive responses to imagined events. It was hypothesised that anticipated pleasure, anticipatory pleasure and positive affect would be higher in an outcome-focused task relative to a process-focused task. Further, ratings of perceived control and likelihood of the future event will be higher after a process-focused task relative to the outcome-focused.
METHODS: Participants ( = 134; M = 35.1 years (age), SD = 13.1) generated personally relevant future events online, were randomly assigned to focus on either outcomes or the steps required to achieve them, and completed pre-post questionnaires relating to these future events.
RESULTS: Outcome-focused thinking increased anticipatory pleasure, motivation and personal significance. In contrast, process-focused thinking reduced perceived control and was associated with reductions in both anticipated and anticipatory pleasure. No effects were observed for perceived likelihood, and positive affect increased modestly across conditions.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that outcome-focused future thinking enhances affective engagement, whereas process-focused thinking may introduce constraints that attenuate perceived control and reward-related responses. Distinguishing between these modes of future thinking has implications for models of motivation and interventions targeting future-oriented cognition.
